title: A girl and a woman (Matthew 9:14–26)
hook: new wine, a bleeding woman, and a ruler's daughter taken by the hand
tomorrow: when the need is huge, what's the first move?

segments.voice: Yesterday, go and learn: mercy, not sacrifice, at a table full of the wrong guests. Today, two people need him at once.

Two calls come in at once, and you can only pick up one. Matthew tells a day like that. A ruler kneels: "My daughter is even now dead: but come and lay thy hand upon her, and she shall live." Jesus gets up and goes. On the way, in the crush of the crowd, a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years reaches from behind and touches the hem of his garment. Matthew folds one story inside the other.
screen: `TWO CALLS AT ONCE.` → `A RULER KNEELS.` → `A HAND ON HIS HEM.`

segments.voice: Just before this, Jesus says new wine goes into new bottles. Here's what new feels like: a hand. The woman has a plan she says only to herself: "If I may but touch his garment, I shall be whole." Fingers on the edge of a cloak, from behind, hoping that's the end of it. But Jesus turns, sees her, and speaks: "Daughter, be of good comfort; thy faith hath made thee whole." Daughter. He's on his way to a ruler's daughter, and he stops to give a stranger the same name. Then the ruler's house: minstrels, a noisy crowd, mourning already under way. Jesus says: "Give place: for the maid is not dead, but sleepeth." And the King James puts it plainly: "they laughed him to scorn." He sends the crowd outside. Then three short clauses: "he went in, and took her by the hand, and the maid arose." Notice the two touches. The woman reaches for his clothes in secret; Jesus reaches for the girl's hand behind a closed door. One hand reaching up, one hand reaching down. Neither is pushed away. A girl and a woman, both called daughter, and both of them get up.
screen: `NEW WINE, NEW BOTTLES.` · `A TOUCH ON THE HEM.` · `DAUGHTER, BE OF GOOD COMFORT.` · `TOOK HER BY THE HAND.` · then, large: `SHE AROSE.`

segments.voice: Rest one hand open on your knee, palm up. With the other, take it gently by the wrist, the way you'd help someone stand, and feel the warmth there. Stay with that grip, and let one person come to mind whose hand you could take this week.
A girl and a woman. One touch from behind in a crowd, one hand taken behind a closed door, and both get up.
screen: `A GIRL AND A WOMAN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: she arose. Two daughters, two touches, and nobody in this story pushed away. Rest well.

screen: `DAY 1439 COUNTS.` → `MATTHEW, READ THROUGH · 13 OF 60.` → `TOMORROW: WHEN THE NEED IS HUGE, WHAT'S THE FIRST MOVE?`

howItsDone: Christians read this pair of healings in more than one way: as signs of who Jesus is, as a picture of faith reaching out, and, for some, as a foretaste of resurrection.

fork.setup: a classmate just got awful news and sits frozen on the hallway floor. you have no idea what to say. what fits today's story?
options: sit beside her and offer a hand or a shoulder.

fork.reveal: in Matthew a touch says what words can't: a hand on a hem, a hand taken behind a closed door. neither is pushed away.

original.note: Greek: was raised, got up. the word behind the maid arose in Matthew 9:25.

trapdoor: what you thought: she arose is just the happy ending of a miracle story.
what it means: a girl taken by the hand gets up, on the same road where a woman who reached for his garment was told her faith had made her whole.
what a scholar hears: Mark's telling says the girl was twelve, the same number of years the woman had been bleeding; Matthew keeps it short and sets both scenes on one road.
guess: a healed woman and a raised girl, told as one story
two sisters who followed Jesus from town to town
a mother and daughter who argued about fasting
recall: what God desires more than offerings
Jesus baptized in line with everyone

chat.says: Dale just showed up on Pop's porch. nobody talked. Pop held out his hand. is that enough??
options: In Matthew a touch said what words couldn't. A held-out hand is a real start, not the end.
Not without a full apology. Jesus always gave a speech before he touched anyone.
It means everything's fixed. The girl arose, and the story was over for everyone.
chat.meaning: The woman touched his hem in secret; Jesus took the girl by the hand. Neither was pushed away, and the touch came before any speech.

minstrels.meaning: musicians, here playing for a funeral

notes: 'Twelve years' of bleeding is from Matthew 9:20. The girl's age (twelve) is only in Mark 5:42 and appears only in the trapdoor's scholar floor, attributed to Mark.
'bottles' glossed as skin containers for wine (wineskins), the usual reading of the KJV word here; confirm.
The 'kneels' in the hook renders KJV 'worshipped him' (9:18); confirm the paraphrase.
howItsDone gives three readings (sign, faith, foretaste of resurrection) without ranking; confirm fair.
